course: AP Biology - Information, Energetics, Evolution and Systems
attribution: Original scope and sequence authored for the Luminfest Learning Harness, dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
scope: Structure only: concept titles, unit order and prerequisite intent. No third-party curriculum text is reproduced, and no restricted source is ingested.
description: A college-level biology course organised around the AP framework: the chemistry of water and macromolecules, cell structure and membrane transport, enzymes, photosynthesis and respiration, signal transduction and the cell cycle, meiosis and inheritance, gene expression and biotechnology, natural selection and phylogeny, and the ecology of populations, communities and ecosystems.

topics.topic: Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

concepts.title: Water as a Polar Solvent
concepts.summary: Oxygen's higher electronegativity gives water a partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positives on its hydrogens, so water surrounds ions and polar molecules in a hydration shell, which is why salts dissolve while oils do not.

concepts.title: Cohesion, Adhesion and Capillary Action
concepts.summary: Water hydrogen-bonds to itself (cohesion) and to polar surfaces (adhesion), and that combination pulls water up a narrow xylem column against gravity as long as the column stays unbroken.

concepts.title: CHNOPS and Trace Elements
concepts.summary: Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur make up most of the mass of living tissue, while elements such as iron and iodine are needed only in trace amounts yet remain essential to specific proteins and hormones.

concepts.title: Dehydration Synthesis and Hydrolysis
concepts.summary: Monomers are joined into polymers by dehydration synthesis, which removes one water molecule per bond formed, and polymers are taken apart by hydrolysis, which adds water back at each bond.

concepts.title: Glycosidic Bonds Set Polysaccharide Function
concepts.summary: Sugars are joined by glycosidic bonds, and the linkage pattern decides the polymer's role: alpha-linked starch stores glucose for later use, while beta-linked cellulose resists animal digestion and supplies structural support.

concepts.title: Triglycerides, Saturation and Energy Storage
concepts.summary: A triglyceride joins glycerol to three fatty acids by ester bonds, its highly reduced chains store about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, and saturated chains without double bonds pack into solids while cis-unsaturated chains kink and stay liquid.

concepts.title: Phospholipids Form Bilayers
concepts.summary: A phospholipid trades one fatty acid for a phosphate-containing head, so the molecule is amphipathic and in water it self-assembles into a bilayer with the hydrophobic tails inward.

concepts.title: Nucleotides and Strand Directionality
concepts.summary: A nucleotide is a phosphate, a pentose and a nitrogenous base, and because each phosphate joins the 5' carbon of one sugar to the 3' carbon of the next, a nucleic acid strand has distinct 5-prime and 3-prime ends.

concepts.title: Complementary Base Pairing
concepts.summary: Adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine through three, so each strand specifies its partner and the two strands of a double helix run antiparallel.

concepts.title: Peptide Bonds and Amino Acid Side Chains
concepts.summary: The 20 amino acids differ only in their R groups, and a peptide bond forms between the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid and the amino nitrogen of the next with the loss of water.

concepts.title: Four Levels of Protein Structure
concepts.summary: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, secondary structure is local alpha-helix and beta-sheet hydrogen bonding, tertiary structure is the folded three-dimensional shape, and quaternary structure is the assembly of several polypeptide subunits.
prerequisites: Peptide Bonds and Amino Acid Side Chains

concepts.title: Denaturation and Chaperone-Assisted Folding
concepts.summary: Heat, extreme pH or high salt disrupts the hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold tertiary structure, so the protein denatures and loses function, while a chaperonin provides an isolated cavity in which a new chain can fold without aggregating with others.

concepts.title: Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cell Plans
concepts.summary: A eukaryotic cell keeps its DNA inside a nucleus and divides its interior with membrane-bound organelles, while a prokaryotic cell holds a single circular chromosome in a nucleoid and has no membrane-bound compartments.

concepts.title: Organelles Match Their Functions
concepts.summary: Structure tracks function inside the endomembrane system: rough ER studded with ribosomes builds secretory proteins, smooth ER synthesises lipids and detoxifies, and the Golgi modifies, sorts and packages what arrives from the ER.

concepts.title: Surface Area to Volume Ratio Limits Cell Size
concepts.summary: Volume rises with the cube of a cell's linear dimension while surface area rises only with the square, so a larger cell has less membrane per unit of volume and cannot exchange materials fast enough to keep up with its metabolism.

concepts.title: Fluid Mosaic Model
concepts.summary: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins, cholesterol and glycolipids embedded in it, and those components drift laterally unless anchored to the cytoskeleton, which is why the mosaic is described as fluid.

concepts.title: Integral and Peripheral Membrane Proteins
concepts.summary: An integral protein spans the hydrophobic core and can serve as a channel, carrier, receptor or anchor, while a peripheral protein sits on one face and often links the membrane to the cytoskeleton or to a signalling partner.

concepts.title: Selective Permeability of the Bilayer
concepts.summary: The hydrophobic core admits small nonpolar gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide but blocks ions and large polar molecules, so permeability depends on a solute size, polarity and charge rather than on its concentration alone.

concepts.title: Passive versus Active Transport
concepts.summary: Passive transport moves a solute down its gradient without energy input, whereas active transport moves it against the gradient using ATP hydrolysis or a gradient that was built earlier.

concepts.title: Carrier Saturation in Facilitated Diffusion
concepts.summary: Facilitated diffusion carries a polar solute down its gradient through a channel or carrier, but the rate levels off at high solute concentration because the number of transport proteins in the membrane is fixed.

concepts.title: Tonicity and Water Movement
concepts.summary: Water crosses a membrane toward the compartment with the higher solute concentration, so an animal cell shrinks in a hypertonic solution, swells and may lyse in a hypotonic one, and holds its volume only in an isotonic one.

concepts.title: The Sodium-Potassium Pump
concepts.summary: The sodium-potassium ATPase exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP hydrolysed, which keeps the interior negative and builds the sodium gradient that secondary active transport spends to import glucose.

concepts.title: Compartments Raise Reaction Efficiency
concepts.summary: Membrane-bound compartments keep incompatible reactions apart and concentrate reactants, which is why a lysosome can hydrolyse material at pH 5 without digesting the cytosol around it.

concepts.title: Endosymbiotic Theory
concepts.summary: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from prokaryotes engulfed by a host cell, which their double membranes, their own circular DNA and their bacteria-like ribosomes all support.

concepts.title: Enzymes Lower Activation Energy
concepts.summary: An enzyme binds its substrate at an active site and stabilises the transition state, which lowers the activation energy and speeds the reaction without changing the free-energy difference between reactants and products.

concepts.title: Induced Fit and Substrate Specificity
concepts.summary: The active site is complementary to its substrate and shifts shape as the substrate binds, which is why one enzyme catalyses only a narrow set of reactions rather than any reaction it encounters.

concepts.title: Temperature and pH Optima
concepts.summary: Each enzyme works fastest at an optimum temperature and pH, and beyond them hydrogen and ionic bonds break, the active site loses its shape and the rate falls because denaturation is largely irreversible in the cell.

concepts.title: Competitive and Noncompetitive Inhibition
concepts.summary: A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site and its effect is overcome by raising substrate concentration, while a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers the maximum rate however much substrate is supplied.

concepts.title: ATP Couples Exergonic and Endergonic Reactions
concepts.summary: ATP hydrolysis releases about 7.3 kcal per mole under standard conditions, and a cell spends that energy by phosphorylating a reactant so that the coupled pair has a negative free-energy change overall.

concepts.title: Light Reactions and the Calvin Cycle
concepts.summary: The light reactions split water, release oxygen, reduce NADP+ and build a proton gradient that makes ATP, and the Calvin cycle then spends that ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into triose phosphate.

concepts.title: Pigment Absorption and Action Spectra
concepts.summary: Chlorophyll a absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, so photosynthetic rate peaks at the absorbed wavelengths and the action spectrum tracks the absorption spectra of whichever pigments the plant contains.
prerequisites: Light Reactions and the Calvin Cycle

concepts.title: Glycolysis
concepts.summary: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvate in the cytosol with a net gain of two ATP and two NADH, and it requires no oxygen, so it is the only ATP-yielding stage available to an anaerobic cell.

concepts.title: Pyruvate Oxidation and the Citric Acid Cycle
concepts.summary: Pyruvate loses carbon dioxide to become acetyl-CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle, and each turn releases two carbon dioxide and reduces three NAD+ and one FAD while regenerating oxaloacetate.

concepts.title: Oxidative Phosphorylation and Chemiosmosis
concepts.summary: Electrons handed down the transport chain pump protons into the intermembrane space, and the returning protons drive ATP synthase; oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor, so without it the chain backs up and ATP output collapses.
prerequisites: Pyruvate Oxidation and the Citric Acid Cycle

concepts.title: Local and Long-Distance Signalling
concepts.summary: Paracrine signals diffuse to nearby cells, synaptic signals cross a narrow cleft to one target, and endocrine hormones travel in blood to any cell that carries the matching receptor.

concepts.title: Reception, Transduction and Response
concepts.summary: A signal pathway runs from ligand binding at a receptor, through intracellular relay and amplification, to a response that alters gene expression, enzyme activity or the cytoskeleton.

concepts.title: G Protein-Coupled and Tyrosine Kinase Receptors
concepts.summary: A G protein-coupled receptor activates an intracellular G protein when its ligand binds, whereas a receptor tyrosine kinase dimerises and phosphorylates itself, so the two classes launch different intracellular relays.

concepts.title: Second Messengers
concepts.summary: A second messenger such as cAMP or calcium ion carries the signal from the membrane into the cytoplasm, and because one activated receptor makes many messenger molecules the internal signal greatly exceeds the bound ligand.
prerequisites: G Protein-Coupled and Tyrosine Kinase Receptors

concepts.title: Amplification in Kinase Cascades
concepts.summary: A signal transduction pathway amplifies the original signal because each activated kinase activates many downstream molecules, which is why a single hormone molecule can produce a large cellular response.

concepts.title: Negative and Positive Feedback
concepts.summary: Negative feedback reverses a deviation and holds a variable near its set point, while positive feedback reinforces the deviation and drives a process to completion, as oxytocin release does during labour.

concepts.title: Phases of the Cell Cycle
concepts.summary: Interphase occupies most of the cycle with G1 growth, S-phase replication and G2 preparation, after which mitosis divides the nucleus and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

concepts.title: Cyclins, Cdks and Checkpoints
concepts.summary: A cyclin binds its cyclin-dependent kinase and the complex phosphorylates the proteins that carry a cell past the G1, G2 and spindle checkpoints, and cyclin degradation resets the switch at the end of each cycle.

concepts.title: Loss of Cycle Control and Cancer
concepts.summary: Cancer begins when mutation removes the control on a proto-oncogene or disables a tumour suppressor, so a cell divides without a growth signal and its descendants accumulate further mutations.

concepts.title: Two Divisions Yield Four Haploid Cells
concepts.summary: Meiosis separates homologous chromosomes in meiosis I and sister chromatids in meiosis II, so one diploid cell gives four haploid cells carrying half the parent's chromosome number.

concepts.title: Crossing Over in Prophase I
concepts.summary: Homologues pair as tetrads in prophase I and exchange segments at chiasmata, which recombines alleles that were linked on the same chromosome.
prerequisites: Two Divisions Yield Four Haploid Cells

concepts.title: Independent Assortment
concepts.summary: Homologues orient independently at metaphase I, so a human cell can produce 2^23 different chromosome combinations in its gametes before crossing over is counted.

concepts.title: Random Fertilisation
concepts.summary: Any of a male 2^23 gamete types can fuse with any of a female 2^23 types, so fertilisation multiplies the variety meiosis generated instead of merely preserving it.

concepts.title: Segregation and Complete Dominance
concepts.summary: Each gamete receives one allele of a gene, and in complete dominance the heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype, so a cross between two heterozygotes gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio.

concepts.title: Dihybrid Crosses and Independent Assortment
concepts.summary: A cross between two double heterozygotes at unlinked loci gives a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio, and a significant departure from that ratio indicates linkage or epistasis.

concepts.title: Incomplete Dominance and Codominance
concepts.summary: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype, whereas in codominance both alleles are fully expressed at once, as in AB blood type.

concepts.title: Sex-Linked Inheritance
concepts.summary: A recessive allele on the X chromosome appears far more often in males, because a male carries one X and therefore expresses whatever allele it holds.

concepts.title: Phenotype as Genotype Plus Environment
concepts.summary: Phenotype results from genotype expressed in an environment, which is why genetically identical plants differ in height with light and hydrangeas change flower colour with soil pH.

concepts.title: Antiparallel DNA Double Helix
concepts.summary: The two DNA strands run in opposite directions with the sugar-phosphate backbones outside and the base pairs inside, so a purine always faces a pyrimidine and the helix keeps a constant diameter.

concepts.title: RNA Structure and Catalytic Folding
concepts.summary: RNA uses ribose and uracil in place of deoxyribose and thymine, and because it is usually single-stranded it folds into shapes that can recognise substrates, which is how a ribozyme catalyses a reaction.

concepts.title: Semiconservative Replication
concepts.summary: Each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand and one newly made strand, as the Meselson-Stahl density experiment showed, so replication copies a template rather than conserving the original duplex intact.

concepts.title: Leading and Lagging Strand Synthesis
concepts.summary: DNA polymerase extends only a free 3-prime end, so the leading strand is built continuously toward the replication fork while the lagging strand is built in Okazaki fragments that DNA ligase later joins.

concepts.title: RNA Polymerase and the Promoter
concepts.summary: RNA polymerase binds a promoter, unwinds the template and adds ribonucleotides in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction, so the transcript matches the coding strand except that uracil replaces thymine.

concepts.title: Capping, Polyadenylation and Splicing
concepts.summary: A eukaryotic transcript receives a 5-prime cap and a 3-prime poly-A tail and is spliced by the spliceosome to remove introns, so alternative splicing can produce several proteins from one gene.

concepts.title: Codons, tRNA and the Ribosome
concepts.summary: Triplet codons are read in the ribosome A, P and E sites while tRNA delivers the amino acid matched to each codon, and the code is redundant without being ambiguous.

concepts.title: Initiation, Elongation and Termination
concepts.summary: Translation starts at the start codon, elongates as peptide bonds form between the P-site and A-site residues, and stops when a stop codon recruits a release factor that frees the polypeptide.

concepts.title: Operons and Eukaryotic Control Points
concepts.summary: A prokaryotic operon puts several genes under one promoter so a single repressor can silence them together, whereas a eukaryote regulates the same gene separately at transcription, at RNA processing, at translation and after translation.

concepts.title: Differential Expression Defines Cell Types
concepts.summary: Every somatic cell of an organism carries the same genome, so tissues differ because different subsets of genes are expressed, not because they contain different genes.

concepts.title: Point Mutations and Reading Frames
concepts.summary: A silent substitution leaves the amino acid unchanged, a missense substitution changes one residue and a nonsense substitution creates a stop codon, while an insertion or deletion not divisible by three shifts the frame and garbles every later codon.

concepts.title: PCR and Gel Electrophoresis
concepts.summary: PCR amplifies a target sequence through repeated denaturation, primer annealing and extension, and gel electrophoresis then separates the products by size because smaller fragments travel further through the matrix.

concepts.title: Conditions Required for Natural Selection
concepts.summary: Natural selection acts only when a population varies, the variation is heritable and some variants leave more offspring, so fitness means relative reproductive success in the current environment rather than strength or longevity.

concepts.title: Directional, Stabilizing and Disruptive Selection
concepts.summary: Directional selection shifts the mean phenotype, stabilizing selection narrows variation around an intermediate optimum, and disruptive selection favours both extremes and can split a population in two.

concepts.title: Human Choice as a Selective Pressure
concepts.summary: Artificial selection uses the same mechanism as natural selection but lets humans decide which individuals breed, which is how one wild mustard gave cabbage, kale, broccoli and cauliflower.

concepts.title: Allele Frequencies and the Forces That Change Them
concepts.summary: Population genetics describes a population by allele frequencies in its gene pool, and evolution is any change in those frequencies caused by mutation, gene flow, genetic drift or selection.

concepts.title: Conditions for Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
concepts.summary: Allele and genotype frequencies stay constant only in a large, randomly mating population with no mutation, no migration and no selection, so a measured change is evidence that one of those conditions fails.

concepts.title: Genotype Frequencies from Allele Frequencies
concepts.summary: At equilibrium genotypes follow p-squared plus 2pq plus q-squared, so the carrier frequency 2pq stays appreciable even when a recessive allele q is rare.

concepts.title: Fossils, Homology and Biogeography
concepts.summary: Fossil strata record sequential change, homologous structures reveal shared descent while analogous ones reveal convergence, and endemic island species record long isolation.

concepts.title: Conserved Molecular Evidence for Common Descent
concepts.summary: A nearly universal genetic code, conserved ribosomal RNA sequences and similar Hox gene order across distant phyla indicate descent from one ancestor rather than repeated independent origins.

concepts.title: Evolution Observed Within Human Timescales
concepts.summary: Evolution is directly observable whenever a selective pressure is strong, as when antibiotic use raises the frequency of resistant bacteria within a few generations.

concepts.title: Reading a Phylogenetic Tree
concepts.summary: Branch points mark common ancestors and branch lengths can scale with time or genetic change, so two tips are closest relatives only when they share the most recent node.

concepts.title: Reproductive Isolation Defines a Species
concepts.summary: Under the biological species concept a species is a group that interbreeds to produce viable fertile offspring, so speciation is complete once prezygotic or postzygotic barriers stop gene flow.

concepts.title: Allopatric and Sympatric Speciation
concepts.summary: Allopatric speciation follows geographic separation that interrupts gene flow, while sympatric speciation arises within one range through polyploidy, habitat shift or behavioural divergence.

concepts.title: Maintaining Genetic Variation
concepts.summary: Mutation and recombination generate variation while diploidy and sexual reproduction preserve it, which is why populations retain alleles that selection does not currently favour.

concepts.title: Abiotic Synthesis and the RNA World
concepts.summary: Organic monomers form from inorganic gases when energy is supplied, and the RNA world hypothesis holds that self-replicating RNA preceded DNA and protein, which is why ribozymes are read as molecular fossils.

concepts.title: Cues, Taxis and Photoperiodism
concepts.summary: An organism answers an environmental cue with a directed movement or a timed physiological change, as when a plant flowers only after the critical night length has been reached.

concepts.title: Productivity and the Ten Percent Rule
concepts.summary: Net primary productivity, the energy fixed by producers minus their own respiration, sets the energy available to consumers, and only about ten percent passes to the next trophic level because the rest is lost in respiration, which is why chains rarely exceed five links.

concepts.title: Exponential and Logistic Growth
concepts.summary: A population with unlimited resources grows exponentially, but a finite environment imposes a carrying capacity and growth then follows a logistic curve that levels off at that ceiling.

concepts.title: Density-Dependent Regulation
concepts.summary: As density rises, intraspecific competition and disease lower the per-capita birth rate and raise the death rate, which is the feedback that holds a logistic population near its carrying capacity.

concepts.title: Competition, Predation and Symbiosis
concepts.summary: Species interactions run from mutualism, where both partners gain, through commensalism, to parasitism and competition, where at least one partner loses.

concepts.title: Niche Differentiation and Keystone Species
concepts.summary: Species coexist only if their niches differ enough to reduce competition, and a keystone species shapes the community far out of proportion to its abundance, so its removal reorganises the whole assemblage.

concepts.title: Richness and Evenness
concepts.summary: Biodiversity combines species richness with evenness of abundance, so a community with the same number of species but one dominant species is less diverse than an evenly distributed one.

concepts.title: Habitat Loss, Invasive Species and Climate Change
concepts.summary: Habitat fragmentation, introduced species and shifting climate each raise extinction risk by shrinking ranges and breaking the interactions a species depends on.
